ann_79.text: Through this part, daytime minutes clearly add to the predicted chance of leaving only once they rise above about 188 minutes for customers without a voice-mail plan: for the typical customer, going from 0 to 271 minutes moves it from about 1% to about 9%.
Daytime minutes clearly raise it, and even more so if evening minutes are above 201: going from 112 to 249 daytime minutes moves it from about 1% to about 9%, against about 1% to about 2% otherwise.
Daytime minutes also count slightly more with more than 200 night-time minutes: from about 1% to about 6%, against about 1% to about 3%.
For the typical customer this part acts on (one with about 216 daytime minutes), a voice-mail plan slightly lowers it from about 2% to about 1%.
Across the usual range, more daytime, evening and night-time minutes slightly raise it to about 1% to 4%.
For customers without a voice-mail plan the daytime charge slightly adds to it above about 39.03 US dollars, and being in South Dakota slightly lowers it (on the training data only).

ann_80.text: Through this part, customer-service calls clearly add to the predicted chance of leaving from 3 calls upwards: for a typical such customer, going from 0 to 4 calls moves it from about 1% to about 14%.

For customers without a voice-mail plan, daytime minutes clearly add to it only once they rise above about 188 minutes: for the typical customer, going from 0 to 271 minutes moves it from about 1% to about 9%.

Across the usual range, more daytime minutes slightly raise it to about 4%, customer-service calls (0 to 3) to about 3% and evening and night-time minutes to about 1% to 2%, while a voice-mail plan slightly lowers it.

For customers without a voice-mail plan, the daytime charge slightly adds to it once it rises above about 39.03 US dollars, from about 1% to about 2%; a higher daytime charge slightly raises it and being in South Dakota slightly lowers it (on the training data only).

ann_81.text: Through this part, an international plan clearly raises the typical customer's predicted chance of leaving from about 1% to about 14%.
This part acts on 380 of 4000 customers, 161 of whom left, and clearly raises the typical one's chance (a customer in Illinois with an international plan) from about 2% to about 26%.

ann_82.text: Through this part, a voice-mail plan slightly lowers the predicted chance of leaving, staying at about 1% (on the training data only).

summary.text: For a typical customer, the model gives a clearly higher predicted chance that a customer leaves if the customer has an international plan (about 14%) than if the customer has no international plan (about 1%).

Through one part of the model, the customer-service calls only clearly adds to the predicted chance that a customer leaves from 3 calls upwards: for a typical such customer, going from 0 calls to 4 calls moves it from about 1% to about 14%.

Through one part of the model, total daytime minutes only clearly adds to the predicted chance that a customer leaves once it rises above about 188 minutes for customers without a voice-mail plan: for a typical such customer, going from 0 minutes to 271 minutes moves it from about 1% to about 9%.
The model ignores total daytime calls, total evening calls, total evening charge, total international minutes and total night-time charge.
